abuse.notes:

The fake-payment-notice filter and the daily limit for unpaid accounts keep applying until an account has a payment that is at least 14 days old and has not been refunded or disputed, or an operator has marked the account as trusted. Ask for the password on the confirm page when the browser has no session for that login (or make the link work only in a session of that login), and say in the email "Only confirm if you signed up for GrowSigning yourself just now". Another engineer is editing the sign-in code in src/server/routes-account.ts right now (sign-in with Google or Microsoft): make small targeted edits and re-read before each.

logic.brief:
FEATURE: conditional fields and formulas.
1. Conditional fields: a field can be shown only when another field of the same recipient has a certain answer (a tick box ticked or not, a radio or dropdown choice, a text or number that is filled in / equals / is more or less than a value). Hidden means: not shown, not required, any earlier answer cleared, nothing printed. Rules can chain; a loop is refused when the sender saves, in words that name the fields.
2. Formula fields: a number field whose value is worked out from other number fields of the same envelope (+ - * / with brackets, sum of a list, rounding to a chosen number of decimals), for totals on order forms and quotes. Write the small parser and evaluator yourself in src/lib/ (never eval, never Function); division by zero and empty inputs have defined, plain results (say what on the screen); the result is formatted the way number fields are (another engineer is making number fields accept 1.234,56 and the like today: use the same parsing function if it exists when you get there, grep for it).
3. The SERVER decides. The signing page shows and hides and calculates live so it feels right, but on save and on Finish the server works out visibility and every formula again from the stored answers and ignores what the browser sent for hidden and calculated fields (read applyValues and completeRecipient in src/server/envelopes.ts). The signed PDF prints only what was visible, with calculated values (src/server/pdf.ts).
4. The editor: on a field, "Only show when..." and, for a number field, "Calculate from...", with the rule shown as a sentence ("Shown when 'Has a co-signer' is ticked"). The review step lists rules that can never be true and fields a formula needs that the signer cannot reach. Keyboard and screen reader: a field that appears is announced (aria-live), and Next goes to it.
5. What a signer signed is protected: after someone has finished, changing a rule or a formula changes what their document says, so it goes through the same sign-again choice as any printed change (read printedView and the content version in src/server/envelopes.ts as they are NOW; another engineer is repairing that code today: add to it with small edits).
6. Templates, bulk send (a CSV column can fill a field a rule depends on), public forms and the API (fields[].show_when, fields[].formula, documented in openapi with examples) all work.
7. Tests: the evaluator (precedence, brackets, errors, big and tiny numbers, no code execution through a formula), visibility chains and loops, the server ignoring a browser that lies about a hidden required field or a calculated value, the PDF text, sign-again after a rule change.

comments.brief:
FEATURE: comments on a document, so a question about a clause is asked and answered where the document is, before anyone signs.
1. While an envelope is out, each recipient and the sender can write comments on it, optionally pinned to a place on a page. A comment is either for everyone on the envelope or private between one recipient and the sender (the default for a recipient is private to the sender: people ask things they do not want the other party to read). Nobody ever sees a private thread they are not in: not on the screen, not in an email, not through the API, not in an export for a recipient.
2. Telling people: the sender gets one email for new comments, at most one every 10 minutes per envelope, with the comments in it; a recipient gets one when the sender answers them. The email to a recipient is text written by the sender going to someone's inbox, so the rules that guard sending apply to it: read assertMayEmail, the pause and the fake-payment-notice filter in src/server/envelopes.ts and use them (another engineer is repairing that filter today; call it, do not copy it).
3. The signing page: a quiet "Questions and comments" entry in the menu and next to the document, never in the way of signing; an open question from the signer is mentioned (not blocked) when they press Finish: "You asked <sender> a question that has not been answered. Finish anyway?". The existing "Ask <sender> a question" (grep helpAsked / 'ask' in the signing page) should become this, not live beside it: one way to ask.
4. The sender's envelope page: the threads, who has not been answered, reply, mark as settled.
5. The record: comments are NOT printed on the document and are not part of what is signed (say so on the screen). The audit trail records that a comment was made, by whom and when, not its words. The sender's export and evidence download include the full threads; after completion they are read-only and kept as long as the envelope.
6. Limits: length, 50 comments per person per envelope, rate limits per link; an in-person signer on the sender's device does not see the sender's private threads with other people.
7. API: routes for an API key to list and write the sender's side, documented in openapi; a webhook event for a new comment.

clickwrap.brief:
FEATURE: click-to-agree ("clickwrap"): terms a website's visitors accept with one click, with a record of who accepted which version and when.
1. A team creates an agreement: a name, the terms (plain text with simple formatting, or an uploaded PDF shown as pages), and how it is accepted (a tick box plus a button; optionally only after scrolling to the end). Publishing makes version 1; any change to the terms makes a new version, with a note of what changed, and says who has to accept again.
2. Three ways to use it: (a) a hosted page (/agree/<slug>) with the terms and the button; (b) an embed for the customer's own site: a small script or an iframe they paste, with a short documented snippet; (c) the API: record an acceptance, and ask "has this person accepted the current version?". For (a) and (b) the site passes who the visitor is (an id of its own, a name, an email) in a signed parameter made with a secret of that agreement, so a visitor cannot accept as somebody else; without it the visitor types name and email.
3. The record of an acceptance: the agreement and version (with the SHA-256 of the exact terms shown), who (as given), when, the IP address and browser, and the page it came from. It is never changed afterwards. A person can get a copy of what they accepted by email if an address was given. The team can look acceptances up, filter them and export them as CSV; a certificate page for one acceptance can be downloaded as PDF (reuse the PDF code).
4. Honesty: the page says what is recorded before the click. The hosted page and the certificate say what the record shows (that someone using this browser pressed the button, with the details given by the website) and what it does not (who that person really was).
5. Money and limits: an acceptance is NOT a signature and costs none. To keep it from being abused there is a monthly limit per account, CLICKWRAP_MONTHLY_LIMIT (default 1000), with a clear answer when it is reached and an email to the admins at 80 percent. Put this under "Things to decide before launch" in the README: the owner may want to price it.
6. Abuse: the hosted page must not be a way to show a stranger's words under our name to trick people (the fake-payment-notice filter in src/server/envelopes.ts applies to the terms of unpaid accounts; paused accounts' agreements are closed; a "report this page" link like the one in signing emails). The embed must not let the host page click for the visitor without it being recorded as such (say what the iframe can and cannot guarantee). Rate limits per address.
7. Deleting: acceptances belong to the account and go when it is deleted (read purgeUser / forgetEnvelopes in src/server/routes-trust.ts and add yours; update the lists in src/lib/policy.ts).
8. Remove "clickwrap" from "What is not in it".

encrypt.brief:
FEATURE: encryption of stored files by the app itself, switched on by a setting.
1. Read how files are stored: saveBlob / readBlob / dataDir in src/server/db.ts and every place that reads or deletes a blob (grep blobs, removeUnusedBlobs in src/server/routes-trust.ts, attachments in src/server/mail.ts, the export zip).
2. With FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY set (32 random bytes as base64; say how to make one), every file written is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived for that file, with a small header that says the format version and which key was used. Files written before stay readable as they are, and a script (scripts/encrypt-files.mjs) encrypts them in place, safely: it can be stopped and run again, never loses a file, and checks each one by reading it back before it removes the plain copy.
3. Changing the key: FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEYS_OLD (a list) lets files under an earlier key still be read; the script re-encrypts them under the current key.
4. Nothing may be lost by a mistake with the key: a server started with a key that cannot read the files that are there says so loudly at start and refuses to write new files with it until the old key is listed, rather than mixing keys nobody can sort out later; a file that fails its check is reported as damaged, never served as garbage. With no key set, everything works as today.
5. Files are named by the SHA-256 of their contents today (the same file stored twice is one file, and /verify compares fingerprints). Keep that working: the name stays the fingerprint of the readable contents. Say in the README what that reveals (that two stored files are the same) and what it does not.
6. Say exactly what is and is not protected, on /security and in the README: the files (uploaded documents, signed PDFs, attachments) are; the database is NOT (names, addresses, what people typed into fields, audit trails), so someone with the disk still reads those unless the disk itself is encrypted; the key sits in the server's settings, so this protects backups and stolen disks, not a break-in to the running server. Recommend disk encryption as well. Change the README line under "What is not in it" ("encryption of stored files by the app itself") to say what is now true.
7. Tests: write and read with and without a key, mixed old and new files, a wrong key, a changed byte, a truncated file, the migration script on a folder with all kinds (run it twice, stop it half way by simulating a failure), key change, every reader of files in the product still works (a full send, sign, download, export and delete with the key set: run the existing flow helpers under the setting).

twostep.brief:
FEATURE: two-step login with an authenticator app.
Where things are: src/server/auth.ts, POST /auth/login and friends in src/server/routes-account.ts, and (new today, by another engineer who may still be finishing) sign-in with Google or Microsoft in src/server/routes-signin.ts and src/server/oidc.ts: read how a sign-in is completed there (one shared function finishes every kind of sign-in: find it and put the second step into it, so no way of signing in goes around it).
1. Time-based codes (the standard authenticator apps use: 6 digits, 30 seconds, SHA-1), written by hand with node:crypto. Setting it up under Settings: the secret is shown as text to type and as a QR code if src/lib/qr.ts exists when you get there (another engineer is writing it today; if it is not there, show the text and the otpauth link only), and it only switches on after the person has typed a correct code. Then ten recovery codes are shown once (stored hashed, each works once), with a plain warning to keep them.
2. Signing in: after the password (or after Google or Microsoft), a second screen asks for the code. "Remember this device for 30 days" sets a cookie that is tied to the login and can be withdrawn from Settings ("devices that skip the second step"). A code cannot be used twice. Five wrong codes pause that login's second step for 15 minutes, in words. The answer never reveals whether the password was right before the code was given in a way that helps guessing (think about what each response tells an attacker).
3. Losing the phone: a recovery code signs in and says how many are left; new ones can be made. With no codes left: an owner or admin of the person's team can reset their second step (the person is emailed at once, and it is written down who did it); someone who is the only owner of their account uses a reset by email that takes effect after 3 days, emailed to them at the start and each day, and stoppable by signing in (so a thief with only the mailbox does not get in quietly). Say all of this on the screen where two-step login is switched on.
4. Teams: an owner can require two-step login for everyone in the account; members without it are taken to set it up at their next sign-in and cannot do anything else in that account until they have.
5. What it covers and what not: API keys are not affected (say so); changing the password, the email address or the second step itself asks for a current code; the password reset by email still needs the code afterwards.
6. Tests: the code algorithm against the published test values of the standard, the whole life (set up, sign in, remember device, recovery code, reset by an admin, reset by email with the delay and stopping it), replay, lockout, required-for-team, each way of signing in, API keys, and that no route gives a session before the second step is done.

witness.brief:
FEATURE: a witness for a signer. Some documents (deeds in England and Wales, for example) need a second person who was physically present to sign as witness. The research behind this is in research/gaps.json, key "map:nonus", the need about UK deeds needing a witness (read it and the evidence under "research:nonus").
1. A recipient role "witness", tied to one signer of the envelope. The witness is asked straight after that signer has signed (whatever the signing order says otherwise), is never charged (do not change src/server/credits.ts: read isChargeable there and make sure a witness row does not count; say in your report how), and gets a block the sender places near the signer's signature: witness name, address, occupation, signature, date.
2. The sender either names the witness, or leaves it open: then the signer gives the witness's name and email on their review screen, with one plain paragraph about who may witness (not a party to the document, an adult, physically present; rules differ by country and kind of document).
3. The witness's first screen says what they are confirming, as their own statement: "I was physically present and saw <signer> sign this document on <date>". They tick it and sign. They can say "I was not there" instead, which tells the sender and the signer and leaves the document unwitnessed (the signer can then name another witness).
4. Honesty everywhere it is offered (editor, signing page, certificate, help page): GrowSigning records what the witness states. It cannot check that they were in the room, and whether a document witnessed this way is accepted depends on the law that applies; for deeds, people should check first. No sentence may suggest otherwise.
5. The certificate and audit trail list the witness under the signer they witnessed, with their statement, time and the usual details. A witness at the same email address or the same device as the signer is allowed but marked on the certificate ("same address as the signer"), and the sender is told when it happens, because that is what a challenge would look at.
6. Everything else has to make sense for the new role: declining, reassigning, reminders, the not-opened alert, corrections after signing (changing the witness is not a change to what the signer signed), templates, bulk send, the API (openapi), find my documents, the completed copy. Read how each handles roles today (grep ACTS and the role lists in src/server/envelopes.ts, src/server/routes-sign.ts, src/components/sender/Recipients.tsx).
7. A short, cautious help entry with the date, linking the official source the research cites.

support.brief:
FEATURE: real support tickets: every request has an owner, a history, a status the customer can see, and a published response time that the product holds itself to. (DocuSign's worst reviews are about support: no answer, no reference, tickets closed without a word, nobody owning the problem.)

A ticket has: the reference (keep the existing one), a status (open: waiting for us; waiting: we asked the customer something; answered; closed), an owner (the operator who took it; the customer sees a first name: "Maya is looking at this"), a priority decided by the topic (cannot sign in, charged wrongly, a document is stuck or a deadline is near: urgent; everything else: normal), and a thread: every message from the customer and from operators with its time, plus internal notes only operators see. Keep what exists working (the form, the acknowledgement email, the reference, signer requests that also reach the sender).
2. Published response times, in src/lib/policy.ts and settable: SUPPORT_FIRST_REPLY_HOURS (default 24) and SUPPORT_URGENT_REPLY_HOURS (default 8), counted in real hours (say so). The help page, the acknowledgement email and the ticket itself say the actual time by which a person will have answered ("by Tuesday 14:00" in the reader's time zone where known, otherwise UTC and said so). When we are late the ticket says so honestly to the customer ("We are late with this. Sorry. It has been passed to ..."), the timer emails the operators once per overdue ticket (escalation), and the operator queue shows late ones first. If no operator can be reached at all (see supportWarning) the form must keep saying what it says today.

The email has a private link to the ticket (a secret in the link, stored hashed) that works WITHOUT a login, because the people who need support most are locked out: there they read the whole thread, reply, and mark it solved. Signed-in people also see all their tickets under Help ("Your requests") with status, owner, due time and thread, and can reply there. A reply to an answered or closed ticket reopens it (within 30 days of closing; after that it opens a new one that links to the old). signin.brief:
FEATURE: sign in and sign up with Google or Microsoft, next to email and password.
Where things are: src/server/auth.ts (sessions, cookies), POST /auth/signup and /auth/login in src/server/routes-account.ts (note what login does after the password check: restores a closing login, accepts an invitation, opens the workspace used last, makes a workspace for someone who has none; and what signup does: ownWorkspace, welcome signatures once, invitation, free-plan code through redeemCode), pages src/app/login/page.tsx, src/app/signup/page.tsx, src/components/AuthForm.tsx, the settings page (src/app/app/settings/page.tsx, the tab with profile and password).
What to build:
1. Settings: GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID + GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID + MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET (+ MICROSOFT_TENANT, default "common"). A provider is on only when both of its values are set. A public route tells the pages which are on; with none on, the pages look exactly as today.
2. The standard authorization-code flow with OpenID Connect, by hand with fetch: state (bound to the browser by a short-lived HttpOnly cookie, single use), nonce, PKCE (S256). The callback exchanges the code, then VERIFIES THE ID TOKEN ITSELF: signature (RS256) against the provider's published keys (fetch the JWKS, cache it for an hour, refetch once on an unknown key id), issuer, audience, expiry, nonce. Use node:crypto (createPublicKey from a JWK, verify). For Microsoft with a multi-tenant app the issuer is per tenant: check it against the token's own tid (https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0).
3. Who is this person? An identity is (provider, subject): for Google the "sub" claim, for Microsoft "tid" + "oid" (or "sub"). Keep them in a new table (provider, subject, user_id, email, created_at) UNIQUE(provider, subject). NEVER identify a person by the email in the token alone: a Microsoft "email" claim can be set by the account's own admin to anything (this is the known "nOAuth" account-takeover). Rules:
   - Known identity: sign that user in.
   - Unknown identity, and a user with that email exists: link and sign in ONLY if the provider vouches for the address (Google: email_verified === true; Microsoft: the optional claim xms_edov === true). Otherwise do not sign in: send the person to the login page with a plain explanation ("You already have a GrowSigning login with this address. Sign in with your password once, then connect Microsoft under Settings."). Tell the existing user by email when a new sign-in method is connected to their login, whichever way it happened.
   - Unknown identity and no such user: create the login exactly as sign-up does (own workspace, welcome signatures once, an invitation carried through the flow joins the team instead, a free-plan code typed on the sign-up page is carried through and redeemed). email_verified is 1 only if the provider vouches; otherwise send our own confirmation email as sign-up does. The password is unusable until the person sets one (the "forgot password" flow must work for them and must say something sensible).
   - Everything password login does after the password check also happens here (factor it into one shared function instead of copying it): restoring a login that is being closed, the invitation, last workspace, a workspace for someone removed from their only team. Rate limits per address as for login.
4. The buttons: "Continue with Google" / "Continue with Microsoft" on the login and sign-up pages (invitation and code in the URL are carried through), with the providers' names in plain text (no logos to license). Errors come back to the page in words (cancelled at the provider; the address is not confirmed there; this address already has a login; the link was used twice or took too long).
5. Settings: a "Ways to sign in" part: password (set / not set yet, with a way to set one), Google and Microsoft (connected as which address, since when; Connect; Disconnect). Disconnecting the last way in is refused with words that say why. Connecting while signed in runs the same flow and links to the signed-in user (refuse if that identity already belongs to another login). API keys can do none of this (see PERSON_ONLY in src/server/router.ts).
6. Tests with a stand-in provider: generate an RSA key in the test, serve the JWKS and the token endpoint through a fetch stub, sign ID tokens yourself. Cover at least: happy path new person (Google and Microsoft); returning person; state missing, wrong, reused; nonce wrong; wrong audience; wrong issuer (and the Microsoft tid rule); expired; bad signature; alg "none" and HS256 signed with the public key (both must be refused); unverified address must not take over an existing login (both providers); verified address links and the owner is told; invitation joins the team; free code redeemed; closing login restored; removed member gets a workspace; disconnect rules; provider not configured means no route works and no button is shown; the redirect after sign-in can only go to a path on this site (no open redirect).
7. Docs: README (settings table, the exact redirect addresses to register with each provider: APP_URL + the callback path), .env.example, the security page (how identity is decided, in two sentences), help page.

signercode.brief:
FEATURE: checking who is signing with a one-time code, by email or by text message, and text messages as a second way to reach a signer.
Where things are: recipients and their access code (a shared secret the sender tells the signer another way) in src/server/envelopes.ts and src/server/routes-sign.ts (find(), the tries and the lock, how a device that passed is remembered), the signing page src/app/sign/[token]/page.tsx and src/components/sign/*, the editor's recipient rows (src/components/editor/StepAdd.tsx, src/components/sender/Recipients.tsx), the certificate of completion in src/server/pdf.ts, the audit trail (audit()), the abuse limits that guard every new person who is emailed (assertMayEmail and the "reached" table in envelopes.ts, unpaidDailyRecipients in src/lib/policy.ts), correctEnvelope / correctRecipient / reassignRecipient, the outbox.
What to build:
1. Per recipient the sender can ask for a check before the document opens: none (as today), the existing access code, a one-time code sent to the recipient's email address at the moment of signing, or a one-time code sent by text message to a mobile number the sender typed for that recipient. API: recipients[].verify = "none" | "email_code" | "sms_code", recipients[].phone (E.164, validated, kept only on that recipient). The existing access code keeps working as it does and can be combined with a one-time code.
2. Text messages go out through a provider chosen by settings, by fetch: (a) Twilio (TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID, TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN, and TWILIO_FROM or TWILIO_MESSAGING_SERVICE_SID), (b) any other provider through a small generic hook: SMS_WEBHOOK_URL gets a POST with JSON { to, text } and "Authorization: Bearer SMS_WEBHOOK_TOKEN". Without either, text messages do not exist in the product: the editor does not offer them, the API refuses verify "sms_code" and phone-based notices with a sentence that says the operator of this server has not switched text messages on. In development and tests texts go to an outbox table like emails do (show them on the dev outbox page too). A failed send is retried like a failed email (read how mail retry works in mail.ts and the timer) and the sender is told if it never goes through.
3. The code: 6 digits from crypto.randomInt, stored hashed, valid 10 minutes, at most 5 wrong tries per code (then a new one must be requested), a new code at most once a minute and 5 an hour per recipient and also limited per caller address, compared in constant time. Asking for a code never reveals the full address or number to whoever holds the link: show it masked (j***@example.com, +44 *** *** 4321). A device that passed stays passed for that link the same way a correct access code is remembered now (reuse that mechanism; read it first). No part of the document, its name, the other recipients or the sender's message is shown before the check is passed (check what GET /sign/:token returns before the access code today and keep to the same or less).
4. The signing page: the code screen, in plain words, usable on a phone with the numeric keypad and one-time-code autofill (autocomplete="one-time-code", inputmode="numeric"), a "send a new code" button that says when it can be used again, and a way out when the code never arrives ("This is not my number", "I do not get the code": tells the sender through the existing problem alerts and tells the signer honestly that the sender has to fix it).
5. The record: the audit trail gets a line when a code is sent (masked destination, the channel), when a wrong code is tried, and when the check is passed; the certificate of completion says for each signer how they were checked ("One-time code sent by text message to +44 *** *** 4321, passed 12 March 2026 14:02 UTC"), and "Link sent by email only" when there was no check, so nobody reads more into it than happened. The security page and help page explain in two sentences what each check proves and what it does not (a code sent to the same mailbox as the link proves less than a text to a phone).
6. Text message notices: when a recipient has a phone number and texts are on, the sender can also choose "also text the signing link" for that recipient (off by default). The text is short, names the sender and the document, says it is from GrowSigning for that sender, and carries the link. Reminders follow at most once a day. The abuse rules count a text like an email to that person (the same daily limits, the pause, the fake-payment-notice filter over the text), and a recipient who reports the document or declines gets no more texts.
7. Corrections: changing a recipient's phone number or check through the existing correction calls works, resets any passed check for that recipient and is written to the audit trail; swapping the person does too. Templates, bulk send (a "phone" column in the CSV) and public forms: decide and document what each supports (public form visitors type their own details, so a text code there checks only that they hold that phone: allow email_code and sms_code only if you can do it safely, otherwise refuse with words).
8. Money: a text costs the operator money. Add SMS_DAILY_PER_ACCOUNT (default 200) as a hard stop per account per day with a clear refusal, and count resends. Do not touch billing: texts are not charged to customers.
9. Tests with the provider stubbed (and the outbox): every rule above, the refusals, masked values, what is returned before the check, the limits, corrections, the certificate text (extract the PDF text the way other tests do), texts not offered when not configured, Twilio and the generic hook each called with the right body and credentials, a provider failure, and that an API caller cannot read the code from any answer.
10. Docs: README (settings table and a short "Checking who signs" section), .env.example, openapi (the new fields), developers page, help and security pages.

bounces.brief:
FEATURE: knowing when an email did not arrive, and doing something about it. Today only the hand-over to the mail server is known (src/server/mail.ts: read all of it, including the retry of failed sends and what the audit trail says when).
What to build:
1. Every outgoing email gets an id of ours that the mail provider will echo back: a Message-ID we generate and store, and a header X-SG-Mail with the row id of the emails table (add columns to emails: message_id, recipient_id where the mail is about a recipient, delivered_at, bounced_at, bounce_kind, bounce_reason, complained_at). Look at how nodemailer or the SMTP code here sets headers.
2. A public route for delivery events from the mail provider: POST /mail/events, authorised by a secret (MAIL_EVENTS_TOKEN: accept it as ?token=..., as "Authorization: Bearer ..." or as HTTP Basic password; compare in constant time; without the setting the route answers 404 and the product says nowhere that it tracks bounces). It understands, by looking at the body: a plain shape of our own ({ type: "bounce" | "soft_bounce" | "complaint" | "delivered", email, message_id?, mail_id?, reason? } or an array of those), and the bounce/complaint/delivery webhooks of Postmark, SendGrid (event array), Mailgun, Resend, and Amazon SES through SNS (a Notification whose Message is JSON; a SubscriptionConfirmation is confirmed by fetching SubscribeURL only if its host ends in .amazonaws.com). Look the formats up from memory carefully and keep each adapter small; state in the README which were written from documentation and never tried against the real service. Unknown shapes are answered 202 and logged once, never 500. Matching: by our mail id or message id when present, otherwise by address for mails sent in the last 3 days.
3. What happens on a hard bounce (the address does not exist, the domain does not exist, the mailbox refuses for good):
   - if the mail was for a recipient of an envelope: the recipient is marked (bounced_at, reason), the audit trail gets "Email to ... could not be delivered: reason", the sender is told at once by email and sees it on the envelope page and in the list ("Could not be delivered") with the existing ways to fix it (correct the address, read how quick-correct and "send again" work), reminders to that address stop until the address is changed or the sender says "try again" (which clears the mark and sends again), and the envelope.updated webhook fires. The "not opened yet" alert must not also fire for the same person.
   - if the mail was to a customer of ours (a login): remember that their address does not work (users.email_bounced_at, reason) and show a banner in the app on every page until they change their address or press "It works now, try again" (so someone whose renewal reminders and receipts are bouncing learns it the next time they open the app; read how the plan and renewal emails are sent in routes-billing.ts but do not change that file), and tell the account's other admins if there are any.
   - a soft bounce (mailbox full, try later) is noted on the mail and in the audit trail but nothing is stopped, unless the same address soft-bounced on 3 separate days: then treat it as hard.
4. A complaint (the person marked our mail as spam): never mail that address again about that envelope (the recipient is marked, reminders stop, the sender is told what happened and that only the recipient can undo it by asking), and count it as a report against the sending account the way the "report this email" link does (read how abuse reports count towards a pause in envelopes.ts / routes-trust.ts and reuse it, do not duplicate it).
5. A do-not-mail list across envelopes: an address that hard-bounced is not mailed again by any NEW envelope of the same account for 30 days without the sender seeing a clear warning at send time ("x@y.z bounced on 3 May: no such mailbox. Check the address."), with a way to send anyway. Never refuse silently and never drop a mail without telling the person who wanted it sent.
6. "Delivered" events fill delivered_at and let the envelope page say "Delivered to the mail server of example.com" instead of only "Sent"; without such events the page says what it says today. Do not claim "read".
7. The mail log an operator can look at: the dev outbox page already lists stored mails; make the status there show delivered, bounced and complained. Stored copies of mails are deleted on the existing schedule (find it); do not keep them longer because of this.
8. Tests: each provider shape (one realistic sample each) leads to the same result as the plain shape; the secret in its three forms, wrong secret, no setting; hard, soft, three soft days, complaint, delivered; matching by id and by address; the sender's email and the envelope answers; reminders stop and start again; the banner facts for a bouncing login (GET /me) and clearing it; the warning at send time and sending anyway; events for unknown mails; a huge or malformed body; the SNS confirmation only for amazonaws.com.
9. Docs: README (setting, the address to give each provider, which providers), .env.example, openapi if API users see new fields (recipients[].bounced_at and so on: yes, document them), help page (what "Could not be delivered" means and what to do), security page if relevant.

tplroles.brief:
FEATURE: permissions per template. Today (read it: src/server/routes-envelopes.ts and envelopes.ts, grep "template"; tests/lifecycle.test.ts 'members use every template but change only their own') every member can use every template and only the person it belongs to or an admin can change or delete it. Teams ask for more: some templates are for HR only, some may be changed by a few people, some are locked so nobody sends an altered contract.
What to build:
1. Per template three settings, changeable by the person the template belongs to and by admins:
   - who can use it: everyone on the team (default, as today) / admins only / chosen members;
   - who can change it: its owner and admins (default, as today) / chosen members as well / everyone on the team;
   - locked wording, yes or no: when yes, an envelope started from the template by someone who cannot change the template may fill in recipients and their own fields' values but cannot change the documents, the fixed text, the fields or the message (decide the exact line by reading what an envelope made from a template can edit before sending, keep it simple, and say on screen what is locked and who can unlock it).
   Store it on the template (new columns, and a small table for chosen members). Admins and the owner of the account can always use and change everything, so nothing is ever locked away from the people responsible for the account.
2. Enforce it everywhere a template is read, used or changed, for a browser and for an API key (a key acts as the person who made it): the list of templates (ones you cannot use are not listed), reading one, starting an envelope from one, bulk send, creating or editing a public form from one (who may publish a template to strangers: only people who can change it), copying one (a copy of a template you can only use must not become a way around the lock: the copy keeps the lock and the same people), deleting, and the hand-over when a member is removed or leaves (POST /account/leave and DELETE /account/members/:id in src/server/routes-account.ts: their chosen-member entries go, their templates pass to the successor as today). A refusal says who to ask ("Ask Maya Lopez or an admin").
3. Screens: on the template page (src/app/app/templates/page.tsx and the template editor) a "Who can use this" part that shows the current rule in a sentence, lets the people allowed change it, with the member list for "chosen members"; the list shows a small lock or "Admins only" mark; the envelope editor, when the wording is locked, shows the locked parts as locked and says why, instead of letting people edit and refusing at the end.
4. Tests: every route above for an owner, an admin, the template's owner, a chosen member, another member, and an API key of each; the lock (through the editor's save call and through the plain API); the copy rule; bulk and public forms; hand-over and leaving; an existing database (templates made before this have the defaults); changing the rule is itself only for owner/admins and is written to the template's history if templates have one (grep audit).
5. Docs: README (features list and "How it is built" if a table is added), openapi (the new fields on templates), developers page, help page.

stamp.brief:
FEATURE: stamps. Many businesses (in much of Africa, Asia, Latin America and Europe) put a company stamp or seal next to a signature, and some documents are not accepted without one. The owner asked: upload a design for a stamp, and make sure it actually LOOKS LIKE A STAMP on the document, like ink from a rubber stamp, not a picture pasted on top.
1. Uploading a design. PNG or JPEG (and WebP where the browser can read it; refuse SVG, PDF and anything else in words), up to 8 MB, from a file or straight from a phone camera. It may be a clean digital design or a photo of a real stamp pressed on paper (uneven light, shadow, a slight angle, a coloured or grey background).
2. Turning it into an impression (the heart of the feature: do it well). Work it out in the browser on a canvas when the stamp is uploaded, show a live 'before and after' over a real-looking document, and store the result as a transparent PNG; re-encoding through the canvas also strips the photo's metadata. Steps, each with a plain control where useful:
   - Take the paper away: everything that is paper (light, low-saturation, including uneven light: use a local or adaptive threshold, not one global cut) becomes transparent; keep the ink. Trim to the ink, with a small margin.
   - One ink colour, as real stamps have: blue (default for most), red, purple, black, green; detect the likely ink from the image and preselect it; the strength of each pixel of ink stays (so thin lines stay thin), the colour becomes the ink.
   - Rubber texture: ink is never perfectly even. Uneven density across the stamp, small specks where ink did not take, slightly rough edges, a very slight softening, never so much that text in the stamp stops being readable at the size it is printed. Deterministic from a seed (store the seed), so the same stamp looks the same in the preview, on every screen and in the signed PDF.
   - A small natural tilt (between -4 and 4 degrees, chosen from the seed, adjustable to 0).
   - Size: a stamp is placed at its real size on the page by default (a round company seal is about 38 to 45 mm across; offer that as the default size for the field and let the sender resize).
   On the page and in the signed PDF the stamp is printed like ink: multiply blending with slightly less than full opacity (pdf-lib supports blend modes and opacity on drawImage; the browser has mix-blend-mode: multiply), so the document's printed text shows through the stamp where they overlap, exactly as with a real stamp. Never a white box around it.
3. Where stamps come from.
   - Account stamps: under Settings, admins add the team's stamps (a name like 'Company stamp' or 'Received', the processed image, the ink, the seed), up to 10; members can use them when they sign or send. Changing a stamp never changes documents where it was already applied.
   - A Stamp field in the editor, like a signature field: assigned to a recipient (a signer or someone signing in person), who applies their own stamp when signing (upload, take a photo, or, when signed in with an account that has stamps, choose a saved one). Or the sender's own company stamp, applied by the sender when they send (then it is wording printed on the page, covered by the rule that protects what people already signed: read printedView in src/server/envelopes.ts as it is now and add to it with a small edit).
   - Required or optional, like other fields. 'Finish later' keeps an applied stamp, as it keeps a signature.
4. The record. The audit trail says who applied which stamp to which field and when (with a fingerprint of the image), and the certificate of completion lists it under that person. Honest words everywhere it is offered: a stamp here is a picture of a stamp that this person put on the document; GrowSigning does not check that the person may use it, and it is not a certified electronic seal. Never suggest more.
5. Where it must work: the editor (place, size, assign), the signing page on a phone and a desktop (keyboard too, labels for screen readers, 44 px targets), the text view, the signed PDF, templates, bulk send, public forms (a visitor applies their own stamp), signing groups and witnesses where they make sense, corrections after someone stamped (sign again, as for a signature), the API (a stamp field type, and the account stamps routes, in src/server/openapi.ts), the evidence pack and export.
6. Abuse and limits: images only, size and pixel limits, one stamp image per field, rate limits on uploads from a signing link; nothing a stranger uploads is shown to anyone but the people on that envelope; the fake-payment-notice rules do not apply to images, but a stamp's name typed by an unpaid account is checked like other names.
7. Money: a stamp is not a signature and uses none. A recipient who only stamps (no signature field) counts exactly as any other signer who finishes.
8. Tests: the processing steps as pure functions where possible (paper removed, one ink, strength kept, deterministic for a seed, trimmed), the routes, the PDF (the stamp is drawn with multiply and the text under it is still in the PDF), sign again after a change, templates, bulk, forms, limits, the honest wording.
9. Docs: README (features, 'What the bad reviews taught us' only if a complaint in research/complaints.json or research/gaps.json asks for it), help, developers page, openapi.

expiry.brief:
Signatures now expire, the way Claude's usage resets each month. The owner decided this on 2026-11-20, replacing the old rule that signatures never expire and roll over. You own the payment code for this task: src/server/routes-billing.ts, src/server/credits.ts, tests/billing*.test.ts, tests/stripe-fake.ts and the Billing() component in src/app/app/settings/page.tsx are yours (nobody else may touch them).
1. Plan signatures (the 9 that come with each month of the $9 plan, and those of the free plan with the code GROWalition) belong to the billing period they come with. At the end of that period (the renewal moment, or the end of the paid period after cancelling) the unused ones expire. They never carry over. The next period brings a fresh 9.
2. Top-up signatures ($1 each) expire 12 months after the payment that bought them.
3. The 3 signatures a new account gets expire 30 days after the account is made.
4. Use order: the signature that expires soonest is used first, so nobody loses one that could have been used.
5. A signature held for an envelope that is out does not expire while it is held; if that envelope is then voided, declined or expires after the signature's own date has passed, the signature is gone instead of coming back. Say so where holds are explained.
6. Store each lot of signatures with its source (plan period, top-up payment, trial) and its expiry; the timer expires lots on time, writes an 'expired' line to the plan history with the count, and the numbers on every screen and in the API are what can still be used. The ledger stays exact: every signature is bought, used, held, returned, refunded or expired, and a test checks the sums.
7. Refunds: the refund rule keeps its meaning for what has not been used and has not expired (refundRuleText in src/lib/policy.ts); an expired signature is not refunded; a dispute or refund takes back unused signatures of that payment first. Write the expiry rule once, as expiryRuleText in src/lib/policy.ts, and quote it on the Plan page, /pricing or the landing page price block, /help, the checkout confirmation and every renewal reminder.
8. Show it like Claude shows its limits: the Plan page says how many are left this period and when they reset ('6 of 9 left, they reset on 3 December 2026 at 14:00 UTC'), and lists top-ups with their own dates. The renewal reminder emails say how many unused plan signatures will expire at that renewal. Top-ups get one email 30 days before they expire and one 3 days before, only if some are unused. No other new emails.
9. Trees: 100 percent of plan and top-up revenue still goes to planting mangroves with Treegens, used or not. The impact numbers count trees funded from revenue (10 per dollar), not signatures used, and say so; nothing on any page may suggest an expired signature plants nothing.
10. Every place that promised signatures never expire or roll over must change: grep for 'expire', 'roll over', 'rolls over', 'carry over', 'never expire' in src/, README.md (the table 'What the bad reviews taught us': change the row 'Prepaid allowance disappears at renewal' to say honestly what happens now and what we do to be fair about it: the date shown everywhere, soonest-expiring used first, emails before top-ups expire), the help page, the landing page and the API description (src/server/openapi.ts: add the expiry dates to the plan and credits endpoints).
11. Also provide, for another engineer who builds the signer's tree note, a function in src/server/credits.ts: paidSignatureFor(recipientId) -> boolean, true when the signature held or used for that recipient comes from a lot that was paid for (plan or top-up, not trial, not the GROWalition plan, not a sender signing their own document for free). Document it in a comment.
12. Tests in tests/billing9.test.ts for every rule above, with the fake clock; run every tests/billing*.test.ts and the whole suite, and tsc. There are no real customers yet (payments are off on the preview), so there is no migration notice to send; say so in your report.

impact.brief:
Make people feel the trees. The owner asked: 'make a cool animation when someone signs or sends their first growsigning, reminding them of the impact. The people who are requested to sign should also know that when they do, 10 trees will be planted.' Decisions: the claim '10 mangroves' is only made when a paid signature is used (paidSignatureFor(recipientId) in src/server/credits.ts, built by the payment owner); when the signature is free (the 3 trial signatures, the GROWalition plan, a sender signing their own document) say instead, softly and truthfully, that GrowSigning gives its plan revenue to planting mangroves with Treegens. Never promise more than is funded.
1. Signers know before they sign: on the signing page, near the top of the first screen and again next to Finish, one short line, for example '10 mangrove trees will be planted with Treegens when you finish. {Sender} pays for it, not you.' with a link to the public impact page. One line in the signing request email too. Approvers, viewers and copies are not told they plant anything.
2. The first time: when an account sends its first envelope ever, and when a person signs for the first time on GrowSigning (no earlier finished signature from that email address on this server), show a short celebration: an SVG and CSS animation, no library, about 2.5 seconds: a shoreline, ten mangrove seedlings rising one after another out of the water line and putting out leaves, the brand colours (forest #1f6f43, deep #134a2c, leaf #6fb35f, light leaf #9ed88f, yellow #ffd24a, paper #f6f3ec; the nib-leaf mark in brand/mark.svg), and the words 'You just planted 10 mangroves' for a paid signature, or for the sender 'Your first GrowSigning is out. Every signature on it plants 10 mangroves with Treegens.' Then a count of what the person has planted so far, from real numbers only.
3. Later times get no big animation: a small line on the finished screen ('10 more mangroves') and the running count.
4. It never gets in the way: it does not block or delay the next step, has a Close button and closes on Escape or a tap, keeps focus sensible, is announced to screen readers in one sentence, respects prefers-reduced-motion (a still picture and the words), has no flashing (WCAG 2.3.1), works at 390x844 and 320x568 and on a desktop, and is shown once (the server remembers it was shown).
5. The server decides everything that is a claim (first time or not, paid or not, the counts); the page only draws.
6. Tests in tests/impact.test.ts: the paid and free cases, first and later, approvers and copies, the email line, the counts; screenshots of the animation at its start, middle and end on a phone and a desktop, which you look at.
7. Green claims law (EU Directive 2024/825, in force since 27 September 2026; the UK CMA Green Claims Code; the US FTC Green Guides): every environmental claim in the product is specific, true and backed by evidence a reader can check, with its source on /impact. Never use generic words ('eco-friendly', 'green', 'sustainable', 'planet-friendly') as claims, never claim carbon neutral, climate positive or any CO2 removal or offset from the mangroves, and never imply a signature undoes harm. Say what happens: the money funds mangrove planting by Treegens planters, whose plantings are filmed and checked by independent verifiers (say so only as far as Treegens' public pages support it; link them). Review every existing impact sentence (src/lib/impact.ts, the /impact page, the landing page, emails, the certificate lines in src/server/pdf.ts 'Signed without paper') against this and fix what does not meet it; the paper, water and CO2e estimates stay only where they are labelled as estimates with their sources.
8. Owner decision for governments: the tree and paper lines stay on the certificate of completion for business customers, and are left off for government tenants. Multi-agency tenancy does not exist yet, so add an account setting 'Leave the impact lines off the certificate' (admins, Settings, Account; default off), which the later government tenancy will switch on for every government tenant. The screens, emails, the animation and /impact are not affected by it.
THE OWNER ADDED ON 2026-11-21 (this wins over anything above about hiding paper figures): "It's good to let people know how much they're saving for this individual sign but not the total since ours is tiny." So: the saving of ONE document stays and is shown where a person sends or finishes it (the review step's box 'Sending this digitally saves about 15 sheets of paper', the sent page, the signer's done screen): sheets, litres of water and CO2e, labelled as estimates with the link to the sources; leave out the fraction of a tree ('0.0018 of a tree') because a tiny fraction reads badly. What is hidden is every TOTAL (the account's 'Paper saved' card and sidebar counter, the public counters on the home and impact pages) until it is large enough to mean something (1,000 sheets; 10 trees planted).

chat.brief:
An AI helper that answers at once, about everything in GrowSigning. The owner asked: 'put an AI chat bot that can help immediately with everything. Use the open source LLM we put in treegens.app.' Treegens.app uses Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI's open-weights model) through any OpenAI-compatible host; copy its approach, copied for you into /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-treegens-app/9d40e5b6-b8c5-5afe-af61-9b17cf0ca38e/scratchpad/treegens-chat-ref/ (route.ts, liveSession.ts, transcriptStore.ts, supportKB.ts, SupportChat.tsx, from the Treegens/treegens-web branch lang-en). Read them; never copy the contact email address in supportKB.ts: our contact address comes from SUPPORT_EMAIL. Decision: everyone gets model answers (visitors, signers, account holders) with limits; past a limit or without a key, the built-in answers.
1. Provider from settings, first match wins: SUPPORT_CHAT_API_KEY (+ SUPPORT_CHAT_BASE_URL, default https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, + SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL, default moonshotai/kimi-k3-20260715), MOONSHOT_API_KEY (https://api.moonshot.ai/v1, kimi-k3), OPENROUTER_API_KEY (moonshotai/kimi-k3-20260715). Send no temperature (Kimi K3 refuses any value but 1), ask for low reasoning effort (OpenRouter: reasoning {effort:'low'}; Moonshot: reasoning_effort 'low'), retry once without those on a 4xx, a max_tokens of about 1200 because thinking tokens count, stream the answer to the page, and fall back to the built-in answers when the provider is down, slow (55 s) or returns nothing.
2. Grounding: the system prompt is built on the server from the same sources the pages use, so it cannot drift: the rules and numbers in src/lib/policy.ts (prices, refund, price rule, expiry, limits, what is kept after deletion, who can see documents), the help page topics, what is and is not in the product (README 'What is not in it'), and a short curated FAQ. It answers only from that; when unsure it says so and offers a person. It says it is an AI and can be wrong, that the rules on the page are what count, never gives legal advice, never says a signature 'is valid' or 'will hold up', never promises a refund or anything the rules do not say, answers in the person's language and says the screens are in English.
3. Never a loop: every answer has 'Talk to a person' under it; one click opens the existing contact form with the conversation attached (the person sees what is attached and can take it off), which makes a help request with a reference like any other. The helper offers a person by itself for: money taken or owed, 'I did not sign this' or a dispute, a security problem, a locked account, anything legal, an upset person, or a second answer that did not help.
4. It knows where it is, not what is in the documents: the page passes only which screen the person is on (signing page, editor, plan page, help) so answers fit; it never sends a document, a name, an address, a signing link or a security code upstream. Before sending, strip anything that looks like a card number, a signing link, a security code or a password the person typed, and say at the top of the chat: do not type passwords or card numbers. Store nothing of the chat except what goes into a help request and counts for the limits; say so.
5. It points to the tools that exist instead of pretending to act: find my documents, find my subscription, stop billing with my card, the check page, the verify page, Fix my name, ask for more time, with links. It takes no action itself.
6. Limits stored in SQLite (one server): per internet address (8 a minute, 60 a day), per signing link, per account, and a daily total (SUPPORT_CHAT_DAILY_LIMIT, default 2000); past any limit the built-in answers, and the person is told plainly.
7. The data page: when a provider is set, '/security' lists it under 'Where your data is' (who, which country, what is sent: only the typed chat) from the same settings, and /security/processing too.
8. Screens: a 'Help' button that opens the chat on the public pages and in the app; on the signing page it lives in the help menu, never floating over Finish or the fields on a phone. A dialog with focus kept inside, Escape to close, answers announced as they arrive (aria-live polite), 44 px targets, 390x844 and desktop, reduced motion respected.
9. README: change the row 'Support is a chatbot loop, and closed to anyone who cannot log in.' to what is true now (an AI helper answers at once, a person is always one click away, the helper hands over by itself); add the settings to .env.example and the README configuration table; add the route to src/server/openapi.ts only if it is part of the public API (it is not: say so in the code).
10. Tests in tests/chat.test.ts with a stubbed provider (never the network): streaming, no key, provider down, empty answer, 4xx retry, every limit, the redaction, the hand-over to a person with the transcript, nothing stored otherwise, and the grounding text built from policy.ts.

ds-lang-core.brief:
Goal: make it possible to show the product in other languages without changing what it says, and record which language each person agreed in. Read first: LANGUAGE_NOTE, consentWording, CONSENT_WORDINGS, consentAuditNote and adoptLine in src/lib/policy.ts; src/lib/dates.ts; the locale columns on users, recipients and envelopes in src/server/db.ts (they exist and nothing uses them: grep locale). 1. src/lib/i18n.ts, no library, safe in 'use client' files: catalogues as flat JSON in src/locales/<tag>.json with en.json as the source (keys like 'sign.finish.button'); t(locale, key, vars) with {name} placeholders and a small plural form {count, plural, one {...} other {...}} read by our own parser with Intl.PluralRules (nothing is ever run as code); fallback pt-BR to pt to en; a missing key falls back to English and never shows the key; dir(locale) is 'rtl' for ar, he, fa and ur. 2. SUPPORTED_LOCALES with a status per language for the interface ('reviewed' by a person, or 'draft' from a machine first draft) and a separate status for the legal texts (consent, what kind of signature this is, the adopt line, witness statements, STAMP_IS, CHECK_PROVES). Ship only 'en' in this batch. 3. Choosing a language: the recipient's language set by the sender, else the signer's browser (Accept-Language) among shipped languages, else English; stored on recipients.locale. 4. Legal text rule: CONSENT_WORDINGS is keyed by version and language. A language whose legal text no person has reviewed shows the English legal text with one sentence in the person's language: 'This part is in English because its translation has not yet been checked by a person.' consentAuditNote records the version and the language actually shown. Machine translation of legal text is never shipped as final. 5. Sender side: a 'Language' select per recipient in the editor (src/components/editor/StepAdd.tsx, state in src/components/Editor.tsx), defaulting to a new account setting default_locale (a small component of yours in src/components/settings/, one line in the settings page); templates keep it; bulk send reads a 'language' column; public forms use the visitor's browser. API: recipients[].locale and the account default, a clear 400 for a language not shipped. 6. <html lang> and dir from the request in src/app/layout.tsx (the signing page sets the recipient's language in lang-signing). 7. Dates and numbers on screen through Intl with the locale (src/lib/dates.ts); do not change what the signed PDF prints. 8. scripts/i18n-check.mjs (npm run i18n:check): every key of en.json is in each catalogue or marked missing, placeholders match, no HTML or links in strings, a warning when a button text is more than 40 percent longer than English. README says how translators can use Weblate's JSON file format. Honest words: LANGUAGE_NOTE keeps saying the screens are in English until a language ships; the sender's own subject, message and documents are never translated. Tests (tests/i18n.test.ts): parser and placeholders, plural rules for en, fr, ar and ru, the fallback chain, a missing key, the legal fallback sentence, the audit line records the language, API validation, the check script fails on a mismatch. Leave out: translating any screen (lang-signing, lang-mail, lang-sender), any call to a translation service from the server. House rules: read before editing, re-read before each edit (others edit too); in shared files (sign page, envelopes.ts, pdf.ts, settings page, db.ts, openapi.ts, README) small edits only, never reformat, logic in your own modules; tables and columns appended in db.ts; new route files imported in src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts and in openapi.ts; settings in .env.example; new words through t() once lang-core is in; plain words, no em dashes; check 390 and 320 px; npm test and npm run typecheck pass; README says exactly what was built.
The government design's language batch (G15) asks for the same foundation; its brief, for what it adds: Goal: signers read the signing page, the emails sent to them, the consent text and the certificate in their language. This is a hard requirement in Canada (English and French) and in multilingual EU states. Start with the signer side, where citizens are.

Build:
1. src/lib/i18n: a small catalogue with ICU-style plurals and placeholders, written here (no runtime dependency) or with @formatjs/intl-messageformat if it fits the bundle. Keys are stable ids, and English is the source. A missing key falls back to English and is logged in development. Dates and numbers keep using src/lib/dates.ts and numbers.ts, now passed the locale.
2. Language choice: per recipient, chosen by the sender (editor and API recipients[].language), defaulting to the tenant's default language, then the signer's browser (Accept-Language) for public forms. The signer can switch language on the page; the switch is recorded, and the agreed consent text is the one shown at that moment.
3. Move every string on the signing page, the signer dialogs, /check, /verify and the emails to signers (request, reminder, code, completed copy, decline notice) into the catalogue. Ship en and fr. Mark fr as 'machine draft, not reviewed' in a translations status file until a translator signs it off, and show nothing to users about that file. The owner decides when a language is switched on for real.
4. Consent text: CONSENT_VERSION gets a language dimension, and the audit trail records language plus version. A language without a lawyer-reviewed consent text cannot be enabled for signers (enforced by a 'reviewed' flag per language in the status file).
5. Certificate: bilingual, English plus the signer's language on the labels, so the document stays readable to a court in either. Values stay as typed.
6. Right-to-left UI mirroring for Arabic and Hebrew on the signing page (dir on html, logical CSS properties), checked at 390 px.
7. html lang set per page, and lang on mixed-language parts (WCAG 3.1.2).
8. LANGUAGE_NOTE becomes true per deployment (built from the languages switched on).

Rules: no string in a signer screen outside the catalogue (a test checks it with a JSX text scan). Legal text is never machine translated into production.

Tests: catalogue completeness for en and fr; plural forms; fallback; the per-recipient language through API, email, page and certificate; consent language and version in the audit trail; a language without a reviewed consent cannot be chosen; RTL screenshots.

Settings: LANGUAGES_ENABLED (default en).

Leave out: the sender app and admin screens (a follow-up batch of the same size), more languages than en and fr.
Build the foundation once: any script (Latin, right-to-left, Ethiopic, CJK) must fit the catalogue, keep all date formatting in one place, and never split names into first and last. Do not add any country-specific locale or calendar work.

ds-convert.brief:

Refuse a zip whose unpacked size passes 100 MB or 20 times its packed size. 2. Two converters, chosen by settings: CONVERTER=soffice runs LibreOffice headless here (a fresh profile folder per job with -env:UserInstallation, --convert-to pdf, CONVERT_TIMEOUT_MS default 60000 that kills the whole process group, at most CONVERT_MAX_JOBS at once in a queue, temporary files removed), or CONVERTER_URL points at a Gotenberg service (MIT) inside the operator's network. With neither, uploads behave as today and the refusal names the file types that need a converter. The converter must run without network access, because a document can point at remote pictures: README says how (a separate user with outbound traffic blocked, unshare -n, or Gotenberg in a container with no network). 3. storeUpload converts first, then goes on exactly as for a PDF (page limit, text for search, scan warning). The original is kept as a stored file linked to the document (encrypted like any file); the converted PDF is what is signed. Audit line: 'Converted from Contract.docx (SHA-256 ...) to PDF by LibreOffice <version>'. The evidence pack carries the original. 4. Words next to the converted pages: always 'Converted from Contract.docx. Check every page: the PDF is what people sign, and conversion can move text.'; tracked changes or comments in a Word file (w:ins, w:del, comments.xml): 'This file has tracked changes or comments. Accept or remove them first: the PDF shows them as they print.'; spreadsheets: 'A sheet may be split across pages.'; outside links in the file (relationships with TargetMode External): 'This file points at outside content, which was not fetched.' 5. Accept list in the file picker and in POST /files; openapi. Honest words: never say the layout is the same; the PDF is the record. ds-seal.brief:
Goal: anyone can open a completed PDF in Acrobat or another reader and see that it has not changed since we completed it, without asking us. Read first: buildFinal and buildPdf in src/server/envelopes.ts (the one place the signed file is made and its SHA-256 stored), renderEnvelopePdf and drawCertificate in src/server/pdf.ts, POST /public/verify in src/server/routes-account.ts, src/app/verify, CHAIN_TRUTH and MATCH_MEANS in src/lib/evidence.ts, src/app/security/page.tsx. 1. src/server/finalpipe.ts: finishPdf(envelope, pdf) runs the steps that turn the rendered PDF into the stored one; today only the seal. buildFinal calls it (one line), so later steps (pdfa, eseal, qtsp, visibility) join here and the stored hash is always of the finished file. 2. src/server/seal.ts: an invisible approval signature (SubFilter ETSI.CAdES.detached, PAdES baseline B-B) over the whole file: add the signature field and dictionary with pdf-lib before saving, a fixed-size Contents placeholder and a ByteRange, save, hash the byte ranges with SHA-256, put the CMS SignedData into Contents. Build the CMS with a small DER writer of our own on node:crypto (src/server/der.ts) with the signed attributes PAdES needs (content-type, message-digest, signing-certificate-v2) and the signing time in the M entry; check each against ETSI EN 319 142-1 and name the clause in a comment. A reviewed library (@signpdf with node-forge) is acceptable instead if our own code does not validate within two days. 3. The key: SEAL_P12 and SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, or SEAL_KEY_PEM, SEAL_CERT_PEM and SEAL_CHAIN_PEM, behind a signer interface (sign(hash) returns the signature) so a cloud KMS or an HSM can be added later without the key on disk. RSA 2048 or more, or ECDSA P-256. 4. B-T: when TSA_URL is set, an RFC 3161 time-stamp token over the signature value goes in the unsigned attributes (src/server/tsa.ts; TSA_USER and TSA_PASSWORD optional). Without it the seal is B-B and the certificate says the time is our server's clock. 5. One line on the certificate, from a function in seal.ts that drawCertificate calls: 'This file carries a digital seal applied by <certificate name> when it was completed. A reader such as Acrobat can check that the file has not changed since. It does not show who stood behind each signature.' 6. /verify: when a dropped file carries our seal, also check it (digest, signature, the configured certificate) and say so; the byte-for-byte answer stays. /security and /security/certificate explain what the seal shows, and that Acrobat shows 'validity unknown' unless the certificate is on the Adobe Approved Trust List or the EU trusted list, which is the operator's purchase. 7. Envelopes completed before this are not sealed again: their fingerprint is in emails people hold. Honest words: a basic electronic seal of the server; never advanced, qualified, or a signature of the people who signed. Tests (tests/seal.test.ts): pdfsig (poppler, installed here; skip if missing) reports the signature valid and covering the whole file; openssl cms -verify on the extracted Contents; one changed byte makes it invalid; a stub TSA made in the test gives B-T and its token verifies; with no settings the output is byte for byte what it was; the stored SHA-256 is of the sealed file and /verify matches it. Settings: SEAL_P12, SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, SEAL_KEY_PEM, SEAL_CERT_PEM, SEAL_CHAIN_PEM, TSA_URL, TSA_USER, TSA_PASSWORD. Leave out: long-term validation and the audit chain time-stamp (seal-ltv), PDF/A (pdfa), organisation seals (eseal). House rules: read before editing, re-read before each edit (others edit too); in shared files (sign page, envelopes.ts, pdf.ts, settings page, db.ts, openapi.ts, README) small edits only, never reformat, logic in your own modules; tables and columns appended in db.ts; new route files imported in src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts and in openapi.ts; settings in .env.example; new words through t() once lang-core is in; plain words, no em dashes; check 390 and 320 px; npm test and npm run typecheck pass; README says exactly what was built.
The government design's batch G05 asks for the same thing; its brief follows. Build the two as one feature; where they differ, follow the one that is more honest and say so in your report:
Goal: every completed PDF carries a standard PAdES signature (an electronic seal) of whoever runs the server, timestamped, which any PDF reader or the EU DSS can check offline. This is the first step from 'a stored hash' to a standards-based file. It is a seal of the operator, not a signature of the signers: G16 adds the signers' own certificates.

Build:
1. Dependencies: pkijs and asn1js (both BSD-3-Clause, pure JavaScript) for CMS SignedData and RFC 3161. No native code in this batch.
2. src/server/pades/keys.ts: the seal key and certificate chain from SEAL_P12 (path) with SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, or, behind an interface G21 fills in, from a PKCS#11 HSM. Expose sign(digest) and chain() so the key never leaves keys.ts. Refuse to start sealing (log, file an operator alert, keep making unsealed PDFs exactly as today) when the certificate has expired, its key usage does not allow digitalSignature or nonRepudiation, or the chain does not build.
3. src/server/pades/incremental.ts: append a signature as an incremental update (a new xref section after the existing bytes), with a /Sig dictionary (SubFilter ETSI.CAdES.detached), a ByteRange covering everything except the Contents placeholder, and an invisible signature field. pdf-lib rewrites whole files, so write the incremental part yourself; pdf-lib may be used only to read. Reserve 32 KB for Contents (enough for chain plus timestamp).
4. src/server/pades/cms.ts: CAdES-BES detached SignedData: SHA-256, RSA-PSS or ECDSA P-256 per the key, signed attributes contentType, messageDigest and signing-certificate-v2 (ESSCertIDv2), and no signingTime (PAdES puts the time in /M). This is PAdES B-B per ETSI EN 319 142-1.
5. src/server/pades/tsa.ts: an RFC 3161 request for the signature value (signature-time-stamp unsigned attribute), which makes B-T. TSA_URLS is a comma-separated list tried in order, with optional HTTP Basic credentials, a 10 second timeout, and the outbound allowlist from G02. The response must verify (status, imprint, nonce, TSA certificate chain to TSA_TRUST). Without a TSA, the seal is B-B and the certificate says so.
6. src/server/pades/seal.ts: sealFinal(pdfBytes) is called once at the end of building the final PDF in src/server/pdf.ts. final_sha256 and /verify then use the sealed bytes, so '/verify matches' keeps meaning 'this exact file'. A sealing failure (TSA down) never loses the PDF: the build retries through the existing finalretry timer, and after the retry limit the PDF goes out at B-B with that recorded in the audit trail.
7. The certificate of completion and /security/certificate gain lines from one constant SEAL_TRUTH in src/lib/evidence.ts: 'This file is sealed with the certificate of <subject of the seal certificate>, issued by <issuer>, at level PAdES B-T on <time from the timestamp>. The seal shows that the file has not changed since it was sealed and who sealed it. It is not a signature of the people who signed: their signatures here are simple electronic signatures with the audit trail above.' The word 'qualified' appears only when the G01 registry says 'qualified seal: held' and the certificate carries the QcCompliance and QcSSCD statements (check them in the certificate, and both must be true).
8. Existing signatures in an uploaded PDF are still destroyed by flatPages() today. Do not fix that here (G07 does), but stop pretending: when an uploaded PDF contains a /Sig field, the editor and the API warn that its existing signatures will not survive. That is one check at upload, in a new function in src/server/pades/seal.ts that G07 will reuse.

Rules: one seal per final PDF, applied last. The seal never changes a byte of what was signed before it (incremental only). Voided, declined and expired copies are not sealed (they are not agreements), and the notice page says so.

Tests (tests/pades.test.ts, no network): make a test CA, seal certificate and TSA in the test, with a TSA answering through a fetch stub. Seal a final PDF. Check the ByteRange covers the file except Contents, the CMS verifies against the chain, the messageDigest matches, the timestamp imprint matches the signature value, and appending a byte afterwards breaks verification. Check pdf.js still opens it. Cover an expired certificate, wrong key usage, the TSA down (B-B then retry), and a key that does not match the certificate. Check /verify matches the sealed bytes. If a pdfsig (poppler-utils) or qpdf --check binary is available, call it in an optional test and skip it otherwise.

Settings: SEAL_P12, SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, TSA_URLS, TSA_USER, TSA_PASSWORD, TSA_TRUST (PEM bundle path). Add them to .env.example and the README.

Leave out: B-LT and B-LTA (G06), validation of incoming files (G07), signers' own certificates (G16), HSM (G21), XAdES, CAdES and ASiC (later, only if a target country needs them: Estonia's ASiC-E is G25's).
Owner decisions that apply to everything built from now on (2026-11-20): the product will be published under EUPL-1.2; no single country comes first (do not build anything country-specific), but nothing may assume Latin script or a family name; plan signatures expire at the end of each billing period, top-ups after 12 months, the trial after 30 days; for government tenants the tree and paper lines stay off the certificate; for government deployments the AI helper only ever talks to a model the agency runs itself. Full research behind this batch: research/docusign-gaps.json (the DocuSign inventory, with sources) and research/government.json.

ds-mail-records.brief:
Goal: a council's records officer or a freedom-of-information team gets a copy of every email the account sends about its documents, and nobody can sign from the archive. Read first: src/server/mail.ts (sendMail, recordMail, deliver, retries, renderMail), how the evidence pack takes links and codes out of stored emails (src/server/evidence.ts), src/server/bounces.ts. 1. Settings, Account, admins only (a component of yours in src/components/settings/, one line in the settings page): up to 5 archive addresses. Each is confirmed by a link sent to it before it receives anything, so nobody can archive into a stranger's inbox; one that bounces 3 times is shown to admins and paused. 2. Every email the account sends about an envelope (requests, reminders, deadline warnings, completed, declined, voided, corrected, comments, witness and group emails) also goes to each confirmed archive address as its own email, never as a Bcc header, with signing links, security codes and one-time codes replaced by '[link removed in the archive copy]', a first line 'Archive copy of an email sent to <address> on <time>', and the same attachments (the completed copy). 3. Archive emails are stored and retried like the others but never count to daily limits, never mark a recipient as bounced, and wait while sending is paused, like the rest. 4. Require TLS: SMTP_REQUIRE_TLS=1 makes nodemailer refuse to hand an email over to our relay without STARTTLS (requireTLS). README and /security say what this covers (the hop from our server to the mail provider) and what it does not (the provider's delivery onward, which MTA-STS and REQUIRETLS on the provider's side decide). 5. /security 'who can see what' lists archive addresses. API: GET, POST and DELETE /account/archive-addresses. Honest words: never say emails are encrypted end to end.
